cards.title: QA Automation Onboarding
cards.summary: A tester who has never written code learns to use VS Code and an AI helper, then writes and runs a first automated test of a website. Ten days, one hour a day.

questions.q: Which keyboard shortcut opens the integrated terminal in VS Code?
questions.why: It opens the terminal inside VS Code.

questions.q: What does the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) do?
options: Runs any VS Code action when you type its name
questions.why: Type what you want and VS Code finds the action.

questions.q: In a terminal, what does pwd show you?

options: Installs the packages a project lists in package.json
questions.why: It reads package.json and installs what the project needs.

questions.q: Copilot shows grey suggestion text. How do you accept and dismiss it?
options: Tab to accept, Esc to dismiss
Enter to accept, Delete to dismiss
Ctrl+S to accept, Ctrl+Z to dismiss
questions.why: Tab accepts ghost text and Esc dismisses it.

questions.q: Why read Copilot's code before relying on it?
options: It can be wrong or incomplete
questions.why: AI suggests, you review: it can miss cases or be wrong.

questions.q: Which command runs a Playwright test suite?
questions.why: It runs every test in the project.

questions.q: Which prompt is better for Copilot, A: Write a test. or B: On /checkout, write a test that checks the total changes when the quantity changes.
options: B: On /checkout, write a test that checks the total changes when the quantity changes.
questions.why: B names the page, the action and the expected result.

questions.q: In an automated test, what is the difference between a selector and an assertion?
options: A selector finds an element, an assertion checks the result
An assertion finds an element, a selector checks the result
questions.why: Find the thing, then check what it shows.

questions.q: Which tool records your clicks and turns them into a starting test?
questions.why: Codegen records a flow and writes a first test you then improve.

nodes.name: automation-plan
nodes.title: The project folder
nodes.text: Everything for the tests lives here.
nodes.like: Like the binder that holds every page.
nodes.inside: Inside: the workflow instructions, the tests, the page cheat sheets and the settings.

nodes.name: .github/workflows
nodes.title: Instructions for GitHub
nodes.text: It tells GitHub what to run, and when.
nodes.like: Like a standing order: do this every time.

nodes.name: playwright.yml
nodes.title: The robot's to-do list
nodes.text: It runs the tests for you whenever someone changes the code, so nobody has to remember.
nodes.like: Like an alarm that rings the moment something changes.

nodes.name: tests
nodes.title: All the checks, in one place
nodes.text: Each file here is one check of the website.
nodes.like: Like the items on an inspection sheet.

nodes.name: smoke
nodes.title: The quick checks
nodes.text: A few fast checks of the most important things. If one fails, stop and fix it first.
nodes.like: Like glancing at the dashboard before driving off.

nodes.name: login.smoke.spec.ts
nodes.title: One check: can a person sign in?
nodes.text: Open the page, enter details, press Sign in, and see that it worked.
nodes.like: Like trying the front door key.

nodes.name: regression
nodes.title: The bigger checks
nodes.text: A larger set that makes sure old features still work after a change. Closed here to keep the picture short.
nodes.like: Like a full service, not just a glance.

nodes.name: page-objects
nodes.title: Cheat sheets for each page
nodes.text: They name each button and box once. When the page changes, you fix one place, not every check.

nodes.name: LoginPage.ts
nodes.title: The sign-in page's cheat sheet
nodes.text: It says where the email box, the password box and the Sign in button are.
nodes.like: Like the labels on a fuse box.

nodes.name: playwright.config.ts
nodes.title: The settings
nodes.text: Which browser to use, how long to wait, and where the website lives.
nodes.like: Like the settings screen on a phone.
